title: Text, regex replace and encodings
summary: Quotes and here-strings, -split and -replace with regex groups, and the encoding defaults that make files look broken between Windows PowerShell 5.1, PowerShell 7 and Excel.

steps.title: Quotes, here-strings and formatting
body: - **Single quotes** are literal: `'Cost: $5'` is exactly that.
- **Double quotes** expand variables and `$( )` expressions: `"Hi $name, you have $($files.Count) files"`.
The escape character is the **backtick**: `` `n `` (newline), `` `t `` (tab), `` `$ `` (a literal dollar).
- **Here-strings** hold several lines. `@'` ... `'@` is literal, `@"` ... `"@` expands. The closing `'@` must
start its own line, at column 0:
```powershell
$body = @"
Deploy of $version finished at $(Get-Date -Format 'HH:mm').
Rollback: ./rollback.ps1 -Version $previous
- **`-f`** formats like .NET's `String.Format`: `'{0,-12} {1,8:N0} KB' -f $name, $kb` pads and adds thousands separators.
- **`-split`** and **`-join`**: `'a,b,c' -split ','` gives three strings; `$list -join ', '` glues them back.
`-split` takes a **regex**, so splitting on a dot needs `'\.'` (or the string method `.Split('.')`).

steps.explain: In a regex `.` means *any character*, so all 8 characters are separators and you get the 9 empty strings around them. Escaped as `\.`, it splits on real dots: `10`, `0`, `0`, `1`.

steps.title: -replace and -match: regex built in
body: `-replace` is a **regex** replace (case-insensitive; `-creplace` is case-sensitive). Groups you capture with `( )`
are put back with `$1`, `$2`, or `${name}` for named groups:
```powershell
'IMG_20261103.jpg' -replace '^IMG_(?<d>\d{8})', 'photo-${d}'     # photo-20261103.jpg
**Use single quotes around the replacement.** In double quotes PowerShell expands `$1` as a (usually empty) variable
*before* the regex engine sees it, and the replacement silently becomes `--`.
`-match` tests a regex and fills the automatic `$Matches` hashtable:
```powershell
if ('shop 4.1.1 by asha' -match 'shop (?<ver>[\d.]+) by (?<who>\w+)') { $Matches.ver; $Matches.who }
Both work on arrays too: `(Get-Content app.log) -replace 'password=\S+', 'password=***'` masks every line, and
`$lines -match 'ERROR'` returns only the matching lines. In PowerShell 7 the replacement can even be a script block:
`'a-b' -replace '\w', { $_.Value.ToUpper() }` gives `A-B`.

steps.prompt: Turn `2026-11-26T08:15:00Z` into `26.11.2026 08:15` (the format a German report wants).
steps.explain: Groups are numbered from the left: `$1` year, `$2` month, `$3` day, `$4` time. Single quotes keep `$3` for the regex engine; .NET uses `$n`, not `\n` like sed.

steps.title: ISO dates in the deploy log
prompt: `~/logs/deploy.log` uses US dates (`11/24/2026 09:02`), which sort wrongly and confuse half the team. Write
`~/answers/deploy-iso.log`: the same lines in the same order, with every date at the start of a line rewritten
to ISO form, **`2026-11-24 09:02`**. Lines without a date stay exactly as they are.

checks.name: dates are ISO, everything else unchanged
checks.fail: The diff shows lines that differ: `>` is what the line should be.

hints: `Get-Content` gives an array of lines, and `-replace` works on every element of an array at once.
The pattern: `'^(\d{2})/(\d{2})/(\d{4})'`. Which group is the year?
steps.explain: ISO 8601 dates (`yyyy-MM-dd`) sort correctly as plain text, mean the same in every country, and are what `Get-Date -Format o` and most APIs produce. When a script writes dates, use `Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm'` or `-Format o`, never the culture's default.

steps.title: Encodings: the 5.1 and 7 defaults
body: A text file is bytes. The **encoding** says how bytes become characters, and the two PowerShells disagree on defaults:
| Writing with | Windows PowerShell 5.1 | PowerShell 7 |
| `>`, `>>`, `Out-File` | UTF-16 LE with a BOM | UTF-8, no BOM |
| `Set-Content`, `Add-Content` | the ANSI code page (Windows-1252 in Western Europe) | UTF-8, no BOM |
| `Export-Csv` | ASCII (`ü` becomes `?`) | UTF-8, no BOM |
| `-Encoding utf8` | UTF-8 **with** a BOM | UTF-8 without; use `utf8BOM` for one |
A **BOM** (byte order mark, the bytes `EF BB BF`) at the start tells readers "this is UTF-8". Linux tools and most
web services do not want it; **Excel needs it** to open a UTF-8 CSV correctly (without it Excel guesses ANSI).
**Mojibake** is what you see when the guess is wrong: `MÃ¼ller` is UTF-8 read as Windows-1252; `M�ller` is
Windows-1252 read as UTF-8. The fix is always the same: read with the encoding the file really has, write with the
one the consumer wants:
```powershell
Get-Content ./legacy.csv -Encoding 1252 | Set-Content ./clean.csv -Encoding utf8BOM
PowerShell 7 accepts code page numbers (`1252`, `850`) for `-Encoding`. For text piped *to native programs*, the
`$OutputEncoding` variable decides: UTF-8 in 7, but ASCII in 5.1, which is why `'Müller' | some.exe` gets `M?ller` there.

steps.prompt: A colleague opens `customers.csv` that your PowerShell 7 script wrote and sees `MÃ¼ller GmbH` in Excel. The file itself is fine in VS Code. What is the best fix in the script?
options: Write the CSV with `-Encoding utf8BOM`, so Excel knows it is UTF-8
Remove the umlauts from the data
steps.explain: The bytes are correct UTF-8; Excel just guessed the ANSI code page because there was no BOM. `Export-Csv -Encoding utf8BOM` (PowerShell 7) adds it. ASCII would destroy the `ü` for real.

steps.title: Rescue a legacy export
prompt: `~/data/customers-legacy.csv` comes from an old system that writes **Windows-1252**. Look at it: `Get-Content ~/data/customers-legacy.csv`.
Convert it to **`~/answers/customers.csv`** in **UTF-8 with a BOM** (the finance team opens it in Excel), so names
such as `Müller GmbH`, `Café Olé` and `Øresund Logistik` come out right. Keep all six lines.

checks.name: starts with a UTF-8 BOM
checks.fail: The file should start with the UTF-8 BOM (`EF BB BF`): write it with `-Encoding utf8BOM`.

checks.name: the names are right
cmd: lines = [l for l in t.split('\n') if l]
for name in ['Müller GmbH', 'Café Olé', 'Señor Pérez SA', 'Øresund Logistik', 'Malmö']:
if name not in t: sys.exit(f'{name!r} is not in the file; it starts: {t[:120]!r}')
checks.fail: Some characters are still wrong (see what the check found). Read the old file with the encoding it really has.

hints: `Get-Content ~/data/customers-legacy.csv` shows `M�ller`: PowerShell 7 read it as UTF-8, and it is not.
steps.explain: `file -i name` (Linux) or opening the file in VS Code (the status bar shows the encoding) tells you what you have. `Format-Hex ./file.csv | Select-Object -First 2` shows the raw bytes in PowerShell: `FF FE` at the start is UTF-16 LE, `EF BB BF` is UTF-8 with a BOM.

steps.prompt: Which PowerShell behaves like this by default?
items: Piping `'Müller'` to a native program sends `M?ller`
steps.explain: In 5.1, say the encoding every time you write a file. In a script that must run in both, `-Encoding utf8` is the one value that means UTF-8 in both (with a BOM in 5.1, without in 7).
